title: 2024 Smart-Meter Electricity Consumption: Verified Findings Report
executive_summary: Analysis of 1,428 cleaned smart-meter readings shows total 2024 consumption of 1,207,699.96 kWh, averaging 845.73 kWh per reading. Industrial buildings account for the overwhelming majority of energy (82.4% share). Demand follows a winter-peaking seasonal pattern, with Q4 highest and Q3 lowest, and second-half consumption rose 4.71% versus the first half. Peak and off-peak tariff energy is nearly balanced (49.65% peak). Notably, commercial consumption shows a moderate negative correlation (-0.64) with temperature, and per-reading consumption is highly skewed (median 406.8 kWh vs. mean 845.73 kWh).

key_findings.statement: The cleaned dataset contains 1,428 readings totalling 1,207,699.96 kWh in 2024, an average of 845.73 kWh per reading.
Industrial buildings dominate consumption at 995,362.16 kWh (82.4% of total), well ahead of Commercial at 196,367.15 kWh (16.3%) and Residential at 15,970.65 kWh (1.3%).
Consumption follows a winter-peaking seasonal pattern: highest in Q4 (352,881.81 kWh), then Q1 (319,677.67 kWh), Q2 (270,277.36 kWh), and lowest in Q3 (264,863.12 kWh).
Second-half consumption (617,744.93 kWh) exceeded first-half consumption (589,955.03 kWh) by 27,789.90 kWh, an increase of 4.71%.
Commercial sites recorded 19 readings on hot days (temperature >= 25 °C), averaging 415.29 kWh per reading.

Per-reading consumption is highly skewed and variable (median 406.8 kWh; sample standard deviation 913.44 kWh). Mean temperature was 11.61 °C, with 62 readings missing temperature. For Commercial readings, temperature and consumption correlate at -0.64, i.e. moderately negative.

Tariff usage is nearly balanced: off-peak energy (608,075.89 kWh) slightly exceeds peak (599,624.07 kWh), with peak share at 49.65% of total. The network comprises 12 unique meters; the highest-use single meter consumed 252,241.26 kWh.

limitations: 62 readings are missing temperature values, so all temperature-based results (hot-day load, mean temperature, correlation) rely on a reduced subset.
The hot-day commercial sample is small (only 19 readings), so its average of 415.29 kWh may not be representative.

The negative commercial temperature-consumption correlation (-0.64) is counterintuitive for cooling demand and may be confounded (e.g. by season, occupancy or industrial mix); correlation does not imply causation.
Consumption is strongly right-skewed (median 406.8 kWh vs. mean 845.73 kWh), so averages are pulled up by large, mostly industrial, readings.
Only 12 meters feed the dataset; results may not generalise beyond this small portfolio, and one meter alone accounts for 252,241.26 kWh.
conclusion: 2024 electricity demand is concentrated in industrial sites, peaks in winter quarters, and grew modestly (+4.71%) in the second half of the year. Peak/off-peak usage is nearly even, suggesting limited tariff-driven load shifting. Stakeholders should prioritise the industrial segment and the single highest-use meter for efficiency measures, and improve temperature data completeness before drawing firm weather-demand conclusions.
